title: India's Sports Budget Soars but Medal Count Stays Grounded
excerpt: The Modi government has nearly tripled sports spending since 2014, yet India's Olympic medal haul at Paris 2024 remained at six — exposing a stubborn gap between investment and international results.
body:
• India's sports ministry budget rose to a record ₹4,479.88 crore in 2026-27, a 72.6% increase since 2021-22, with Khelo India Mission receiving ₹924.35 crore.
  • At the Paris 2024 Olympics, India won six medals — one silver and five bronze — finishing 71st overall, while China won 91 and the United States 126.
  • After nine years of Khelo India scholarships, no national audit of athlete outcomes has been published, according to policy researchers.
  • Analysts say India's sports spending measures inputs, not outputs — and that without performance-linked funding, the 2036 top-ten Olympic target risks remaining aspirational.

When Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a record ₹4,479.88 crore allocation for the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in the Union Budget 2026-27, the headlines wrote themselves. A 15.3% year-on-year increase. The largest absolute rise in five years. A reimagined Khelo India Mission designed to place India among the world's top ten sporting nations by 2036.

But a closer look at the numbers reveals a familiar pattern: spending rises sharply, and outcomes do not follow.

The Gap Between Budget and Podium

At the Paris 2024 Olympics, India sent 117 athletes backed by ₹470 crore in government funding through the Target Olympic Podium Scheme and other programmes. The result: six medals — Neeraj Chopra's silver in javelin, three shooting bronzes, a hockey bronze, and wrestler Aman Sehrawat's bronze. China won 91 medals. The United States won 126.

Since 2021-22, the sports budget has expanded by 72.6%, according to Policy Circle, an Indian policy analysis publication. Over a decade, the ministry allocation has roughly tripled from under ₹1,200 crore before 2014. The medal curve has not kept pace.

"Spending has risen sharply; outcomes have not. The Budget did not explain why earlier spending failed or what changes now."

— Samaksh Sha and Dr Barun Kumar Thakur, FLAME University, writing in Policy Circle

Scholarships Without Scorecards

Khelo India Mission, the centrepiece of India's grassroots sports strategy, now commands ₹924.35 crore — the single largest line item in the sports budget. Its core instrument is a ₹5 lakh annual scholarship, payable for up to eight years. The support is substantial — but not performance-linked.

An athlete stalled at the district level receives the same financial support as one progressing toward the national squad. Nine years into the programme, no publicly available national audit has examined what these scholarships have produced, according to Policy Circle. The only recent independent evaluation, focused on centres in Guwahati and Itanagar, found middling satisfaction scores that do not speak to performance outcomes.

Governance Bottlenecks

Authority over Indian sport is split among the sports ministry, the Sports Authority of India, and dozens of autonomous national federations that control selection, calendars, and coaching appointments — often with limited transparency and frequent legal disputes. Athlete preparation cycles are routinely disrupted by selection controversies.

Australia's Australian Institute of Sport ties funding to independently verified athlete progression through competitive tiers. India's SAI already tracks athletes through a database. The gap, analysts argue, is not technology — it is the willingness to attach consequences to results.

"A top-ten finish by 2036 is ambitious enough to matter and distant enough to test resolve. The test is not what the Budget announced. It is what the Mission measures."

— Policy Circle analysis

New Ambitions, Old Questions

The 2026-27 budget introduces some new elements. A ₹500 crore allocation for sports goods manufacturing under the 'Samarth Pahal' initiative aims to boost domestic equipment production. The Khelo India Mission has been reframed as a ten-year athlete development framework with a nationwide network of training centres at three tiers. Sports science and data-driven performance analysis received explicit emphasis.

SAI was allocated ₹917.38 crore, while assistance to National Sports Federations stands at ₹425 crore. The government has also passed the National Sports Governance Act and the Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 policy, laying out a roadmap for the 2036 Olympics — for which India has submitted a hosting bid.

But The Bridge, a sports analysis publication, noted that nearly the entire allocation is classified under revenue expenditure, with only a small component earmarked as capital expenditure — suggesting limited fresh investment in new infrastructure despite the expanded budget.

What's Next

The government's stated ambition — a top-ten Olympic finish by 2036, potentially on home soil — would require a transformation that the current spending trajectory has not yet delivered. Between the 2012 London Olympics and Paris 2024, India's medal count moved from six to seven to six, even as budgets multiplied.

What remains missing, analysts say, is accountability architecture: performance-linked disbursements, state-level compacts with audited outcomes, and federation reforms that prioritise athletes over administrators. Until those questions are answered with data, Khelo India risks remaining, as the Policy Circle researchers put it, "not a mission — a well-funded intention."
nri_angle: For NRIs who follow Indian sport and contribute through sponsorships or diaspora sports leagues, the gap between government spending and Olympic results raises questions about the effectiveness of India's sports development model.
